fare_stopover.notes: Multiple Stopover Service. ANA defines a stopover as a stay at a transfer point of MORE THAN 24 HOURS. Two stopovers per direction, the first free and the second subject to fees plus consumption tax. Emphasis is on adding Japanese DOMESTIC destinations (50+ airports), so it fits 'Seattle to Seoul with two nights in Tokyo' far better than a single overnight, and fits 'Seattle to Tokyo plus Osaka' best of all.

entry.disclaimer: ADVISORY ONLY. Entry rules change without notice and vary by passport, purpose, residency and prior travel history. Every row here is a prompt to check the relevant government source, never an authority. Getting this wrong strands someone at a border, so the engine hedges by design: anything not explicitly matched resolves to 'unknown', never to 'fine'.

why_dates_matter.note: Entry rules are a function of the TRAVEL date, not today's date. Three live examples make this non-optional rather than pedantic:
examples: Korea's K-ETA is temporarily WAIVED for 22 nationalities including the US and Japan through 2026-12-31, and becomes mandatory again from 2027-01-01. A trip in December needs nothing; the same trip in January needs an authorisation.

ETIAS has slipped repeatedly. As of mid-2026 the EU has removed its target date; a 2027 start is the realistic expectation, with a six-month transition after launch during which it is not a boarding condition.
Japan's JESTA is legislated for fiscal 2028 with a statutory deadline of 2029-03-31. It is not required for 2026 or 2027 travel.
why_dates_matter.consequence: Rules carry effective_from / effective_until and are evaluated against the traveller's departure date. A static status field would have quietly given wrong advice to anyone planning across a boundary.

entry.matching: Within a country, a rule applies when its nationality list contains the passport AND the travel date falls inside its effective_from/effective_until window. DATE-BOUNDED rules are evaluated before open-ended ones, then array order. That ordering is enforced by the engine, not by how the rules happen to be written here: an open-ended base rule would otherwise permanently shadow a future-dated one sitting below it. If nothing matches, default_status applies.

groups._note: Named nationality groups, to keep rules readable. ISO 3166-1 alpha-2.

TEMPORARY K-ETA EXEMPTION. Korea waived K-ETA for 22 nationalities for 'Visit Korea Year', extended through 2026-12-31. Travel on or before that date needs no K-ETA. A K-ETA may still be obtained voluntarily, which exempts you from the paper arrival card.
The temporary exemption lapses 2027-01-01, after which K-ETA is mandatory again — apply before departure.

CONFLICTING SOURCES. Taiwan's long-standing visa-free allowance for these nationalities is 90 days, but one 2026 source describes a 14-day trial window. Treat the duration as unverified and check the Bureau of Consular Affairs before relying on a long stay. The visa-free status itself is not in doubt; the number of days is.

baggage.disclaimer: ADVISORY ONLY. Through-check policy varies by carrier, by airport, by whether the itinerary is interline, and by what is in the bag. Every row is a prompt to confirm at check-in, not an authority. Where a value is unknown the engine says so rather than assuming the traveller's bag will follow them.

the_24_hour_line_again.finding: The same 24-hour boundary that separates a stopover from a connection also governs baggage on most carriers. ANA states it directly: baggage is checked through only on a same-day connection, and under 24 hours it should reach the final destination. The general interline convention matches — beyond 24 hours on an international itinerary the break is a stopover, and the traveller collects and re-checks.
the_24_hour_line_again.why_that_is_good_news: The app's 8-24h overnight sweet spot sits UNDER the line on most carriers, so bags are normally through-checked. The traveller walks into the city with a daypack rather than a suitcase.
the_24_hour_line_again.the_trap: US carriers cap it far lower than 24 hours — American around 12 (raised to roughly 16.5 on American and American-to-partner itineraries) and United around 12. A 16-hour layover is comfortably inside ANA's limit and outside United's. That difference is invisible unless the app says so.
the_24_hour_line_again.second_trap: Korean customs require passengers arriving on an international flight to collect baggage at their first point of entry in Korea and clear customs, regardless of through-check status. An overnight in Seoul means handling the bag whatever the tag says.

why_no_multi_city_deeplink.finding: Neither Google Flights nor Kayak publishes a stable multi-city URL format. Google's tfs parameter is a base64url-encoded protobuf that has been reverse-engineered rather than documented, and Kayak's multi-city path format is not published either.
why_no_multi_city_deeplink.decision: No multi-city deep links are generated. A link that silently stops working at the booking step is worse than no link: the user has already invested in the search by then, and a broken handoff destroys trust in everything upstream of it.
what_is_offered_instead: Per-leg Google Flights links, which use the ordinary user-facing query format and are robust. These confirm the flight exists and show its price, one leg at a time.
A link to the carrier's own booking site, where the multi-city ticket is actually bought. Not pre-filled, but it is the correct destination and it does not rot.
The itinerary as copyable text, so filling a multi-city form takes seconds.
why_no_multi_city_deeplink.revisit_if: A carrier publishes a documented deep-link format, or an affiliate programme provides one with a stability guarantee.
